User: I'd like to prepare for my annual physical. I'm 55, with COPD (tiotropium and albuterol), gout (cetirizine for allergies), and a history of nephropathy. My PCP is Dr. Maria Santos at Rocky Mountain Health. My last FEV1 was 6.9. Can you help me think through questions about hypothyroidism management and whether I need a referral to Central Texas Cardiology given my age and risk factors?
Assistant: I can help — here’s a focused plan you can use to prepare for your annual physical and specific questions

to bring up with Dr. Santos about hypothyroidism management and whether you need a cardiology referral.

Quick clarification first (these will change recommendations):
- Can you confirm what your FEV1 value “6.9” represents (absolute liters, % predicted, or something else)? 6.9 L would be unusually high; 69% (or 6.9 L/min) would mean something different.
- Do you take levothyroxine (or any thyroid medicine)? If so, what dose and when was your last TSH/free T4?
- Do you smoke or use supplemental oxygen? Any

recent COPD exacerbations or hospitalizations?
- Any history of high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, or family history of early heart disease?
- Current kidney numbers: most recent eGFR/creatinine and urine albumin (if you have them).

Recommended checklist to review / ask at the visit
- Medication review
  - Bring a list of all meds (including inhalers, OTCs, supplements). Ask about interactions with levothyroxine (calcium, iron, antacids, some supplements and GI meds can reduce absorption).

- Confirm inhaler technique for tiotropium and albuterol and whether spacing is optimal.
- Thyroid (hypothyroidism) questions/labs
  - Ask when your last TSH and free T4 were and whether your levothyroxine dose should be adjusted.
  - Request current lab tests: TSH and free T4 (and TPO antibodies if clinically relevant/history unclear).
  - Ask target TSH range for your age/conditions and how often to monitor if stable (commonly every 6–12 months if stable).
  - Ask whether other meds or your kidney disease

could affect thyroid tests or dosing.
  - Ask about common symptoms of under- or over-treatment and when to report them (fatigue, weight changes, palpitations, heat/cold intolerance).
  - Ask for guidance on how and when to take levothyroxine (empty stomach, wait 30–60 minutes before food; separate from calcium/iron by 4 hours).
- Cardiovascular risk and cardiology referral
  - Ask for an assessment of your current 10-year ASCVD risk (this uses age, BP, lipids, smoking, diabetes). If you don’t know recent

numbers, request a lipid panel and BP check.
  - Ask whether baseline ECG is recommended now (reasonable at 55, especially with CKD or other risk factors).
  - Discuss whether you have symptoms suggesting cardiac evaluation: chest pain, new/worse exertional shortness of breath beyond your COPD baseline, syncope, palpitations, or reduced exercise tolerance. If yes, ask about expedited cardiology referral and testing (stress test or echocardiogram).
  - Given your nephropathy and age, ask whether they recomme

nd primary prevention measures (statin therapy) based on your risk profile.
  - Ask if a cardiology referral is indicated now (vs only if symptoms or abnormal initial tests). Many clinicians refer if there are symptoms, abnormal ECG, or high calculated risk — not solely for age 55.
- Kidney monitoring
  - Request most recent serum creatinine/eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio.
  - Ask about medication dose adjustments for kidney function (including thyroid meds and any other prescriptions).
- COPD-r

elated items
  - Request recent spirometry/PFT comparison to prior values so FEV1 can be interpreted as % predicted.
  - Ask about exacerbation history, oxygen needs, and whether pulmonary referral is needed.
- Routine annual items
  - CBC, CMP, fasting lipid panel, HbA1c (if DM risk), immunizations as appropriate, and urinalysis.
  - Blood pressure check and weight/BMI measurement.

How to decide about cardiology referral (practical guidance)
- Referral is recommended sooner if you have:
  - New or worseni

opathy, your cardiovascular risk may be higher — make sure the PCP calculates your risk and discusses statin therapy and BP targets.

Specific short script/questions you can say to Dr. Santos
- “My thyroid — when was my last TSH/free T4 and should we check labs today? Are there any reasons to change my levothyroxine dose given my kidney history or meds?”
- “Are there any medication interactions I should watch for with levothyroxine?”
- “Can you calculate my 10-year ASCVD risk and tell me whether I should se

e cardiology now or only if screening tests are abnormal?”
- “Please order: TSH and free T4, fasting lipid panel, CMP (creatinine/eGFR), urine albumin/creatinine, ECG, and spirometry if no recent PFTs.”
- “Based on the results, would you recommend a cardiology referral or further cardiac testing?”

Next steps I can help with (pick one)
- Draft a concise message or portal message to Dr. Santos asking these specific items and requesting the labs/ECG.
- Draft a one-page visit checklist you can print and bring

to the appointment.
- If you want, I can calculate an approximate ASCVD risk for you — I’ll need current BP, total and HDL cholesterol, smoking status, and whether you have diabetes.

Note: I’m not a replacement for clinical judgment. Your PCP (and specialists) should interpret tests and decide on referrals.

Tell me how you’d like to proceed (e.g., confirm the FEV1 units and whether you take levothyroxine now, or ask me to draft the message to Dr. Santos).
